modern: Epicurus says: In my sickness my conversation was not about my bodily sufferings, nor, he says, did I talk on such subjects to those who visited me; but I continued to discuss the nature of things as before, keeping to this main point: how the mind, while sharing in such movements as go on in the poor flesh, may be free from disturbance and keep its proper good. Nor did I, he says, give the doctors a chance to put on solemn looks, as if they were doing something great, but my life went on well and happily. Do, then, the same as he did, both in sickness, if you are sick, and in any other circumstances; for never to abandon philosophy in whatever may happen to us, nor to engage in trifling talk with an ignorant man or with one unacquainted with nature, is a principle of all schools of philosophy; but to be intent only on what you are doing now and on the instrument by which you do it.

Nor did I, he says, give the physicians an opportunity of putting on solemn looks, as if they were doing something great, but my life went on well and happily. Do, then, the same that he did both in sickness, if thou art sick, and in any other circumstances; for never to desert philosophy in any events that may befall us, nor to hold trifling talks either with an ignorant man or with one unacquainted with nature, is a principle of all schools of philosophy; but to be intent only on that which thou art now doing and on the instrument by which thou doest it.

explained.summary:
Marcus quotes Epicurus, founder of a rival school, who said that when he was ill he didn’t talk about his symptoms but kept discussing philosophy, keeping his mind calm while his body suffered, and wouldn’t let the doctors make a grand drama of it.

Do the same, in sickness or anything else. Every philosophical school agrees on this much: never give up thinking clearly whatever happens, don’t get dragged into idle chat with people who don’t understand, and keep your attention on what you’re doing now and the mind you’re doing it with.
explained.today: Being ill or stressed tends to shrink every conversation down to the problem. Marcus suggests you can still talk about books, ideas or other people’s lives, and not let the illness, the deadline or the doctor’s grave face take over everything.
